summary: BBN explains why sites may see messages from IMPs or hosts they thought did not exist: new IMPs are tested on the network at BBN before delivery, sometimes with another number. Hosts do not need to update their tables.

plainLanguage.summary: Sometimes a new box is tested on the network before it reaches its home, so you might hear from a stranger. Do not worry about it.

questions: imps tested at bbn before delivery
why do imps have different numbers
subtitle: Why the ARPANET sees IMPs that don't officially exist yet

tldr.problem: Sites on the ARPANET sometimes receive messages from IMPs or hosts that do not appear in official network tables, causing confusion.
tldr.mechanism: BBN tests all new IMPs on the live ARPANET before shipping them to their final locations. During testing, they may use temporary IMP numbers that differ from the ones they will have at their destination.
tldr.outcome: This is normal and expected. Hosts do not need to update their tables in response to these test messages; they can safely ignore them.

today: RFC 305 is informational and explains a temporary testing phenomenon on the ARPANET. It remains valid as an explanation of how network infrastructure testing has always worked.

sections.title: New IMPs Are Tested On the Network
sections.content: The ARPANET's Interface Message Processors (IMPs) are the network's switching nodes. Before a new IMP is shipped to its permanent location, BBN tests it on the live ARPANET to ensure it works correctly. This is standard procedure.
sections.plainLanguage: Before sending a new box to its home, BBN tests it on the real network to make sure it works.

sections.title: IMPs May Use Temporary Numbers During Testing
sections.content: During testing, a new IMP may be assigned a different IMP number than the one it will have at its final destination. This happens because the official number might already be in use at another site. For example, a TIP destined for ETAC with IMP number 20 was tested at BBN using IMP number 22 (McClellan's number), which resulted in network addresses that do not match official tables.
sections.plainLanguage: A new box might wear a different label while being tested, then get its real label when it reaches home.

sections.title: No Host Table Updates Needed
sections.content: Hosts should expect and tolerate RSTs (reset messages) from these temporary test IMPs. They do not need to update their host tables in response. Official changes are communicated through RFC announcements or updates to Appendix A of BBN Report 1822, the definitive reference on host numbering.
sections.plainLanguage: You can ignore strange messages from test boxes. Real changes come by official memo.
